# `distribution_release_security_support`

`distribution_release_security_support` fails when the security support that
the input `security_support` chooses ends for the node's Debian, Ubuntu, Red Hat family, or SUSE
release within the time you state, or has already ended. The message from `distribution_release_security_support`
names the release and the end date.

The update and release-support checks report waiting updates, a
required restart, and the end of a release's security support. The update and
release-support checks do not look for known exploited flaws.

Use [`apt_security_updates`](apt_security_updates.md) on Debian and
Ubuntu, [`dnf_security_updates`](dnf_security_updates.md) on the Red Hat
family, or [`zypper_security_patches`](zypper_security_patches.md) on
SUSE, for security updates that wait, and [`reboot_after_updates`](reboot_after_updates.md)
for installed updates that need a restart.

To find known exploited flaws in installed packages, including flaws with no
fix yet, use [`known_exploited_vulnerabilities_in_installed_packages`](known_exploited_vulnerabilities_in_installed_packages.md), which reads CISA's list and OSV.dev.

## Set up

Debian and Ubuntu cloud images and server installations may lack
`distro-info-data`. Install `distro-info-data` on the node, as root:

```sh
apt-get install distro-info-data
```

The release dates stay current when apt installs updates to
`distro-info-data` alongside updates to the node's other packages.
MMWatchdog reads the installed files and downloads nothing.

On the Red Hat family, such as Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, and Fedora, the node needs
nothing. The release package installs `/etc/os-release` with the field
`SUPPORT_END`, which the check reads.

On SUSE, such as openSUSE Leap, the node needs nothing. The release package
installs the product file `/etc/products.d/baseproduct`, which the check
reads.

## Inputs

- `security_support` (`regular`, `debian_lts`, or `ubuntu_pro`; required): The security support that the check counts down to. regular: Debian's regular security support (the column eol) or Ubuntu's standard security maintenance (eol-server). debian_lts: Debian LTS (eol-lts), on Debian only. ubuntu_pro: Ubuntu Pro's Expanded Security Maintenance (eol-esm), on Ubuntu only. When the release has no date in the chosen column, the check uses the column eol. On SUSE, such as openSUSE Leap, regular is the end of the release (the endoflife of /etc/products.d/baseproduct), and on the Red Hat family, such as Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux, it is the SUPPORT_END of /etc/os-release. On both, the other two values make the check unknown.
- `fail_when_security_support_ends_within` (duration; required): The check fails when the security support that security_support chooses ends within this time for the node's release, such as 180d.

## When the check fails, and when it cannot check

- **The check fails** when the chosen security support ends within
  `fail_when_security_support_ends_within`, including exactly that time,
  or has already ended. For example, `180d` gives about six months to
  upgrade the release.
- **The check is healthy** when the end of the chosen security support is more than
  `fail_when_security_support_ends_within` away.
- Healthy and failed results name the release and date:
  `this node runs Debian GNU/Linux
  13 (trixie): Debian's regular security support ends on 2028-08-09, in 21 months`.
  After the date, the message says `SUPPORT ended on DATE,
  SPAN ago`. Below 60 days, SPAN is whole days. From 60 days, SPAN is
  whole months, with 30.4375 days per month. The day and month counts are
  rounded down.
- **The check is unknown** when the distribution is not Debian, Ubuntu, the
  Red Hat family, or SUSE, the codename of a Debian or Ubuntu node is missing, the dates cannot
  be read, the release has no known end date, or `security_support` names
  the support of the other distribution. Debian and Ubuntu derivatives are
  unknown even if `ID_LIKE` names Debian or Ubuntu. SUSE and the Red Hat
  family need no codename, and the check reads none. On the Red Hat family,
  a missing or unreadable `SUPPORT_END` makes the check unknown.

An unknown result opens a cannot-check incident once it has lasted for the
check's `alert_after_failing_for`, as for every check
([the failing time](../../how-to/decide-when-a-check-alerts.md)).

## Examples

```yaml
# /etc/mmwatchdog/check_groups/node_software.yml
check_groups:
  node_software:
    check_every: 1d
    time_limit_per_run: 10s
    alert_after_failing_for: 0s
    recovered_after_healthy_for: 0s
    checks:
      release_gets_security_fixes:
        distribution_release_security_support:
          security_support: regular
          fail_when_security_support_ends_within: 180d
        alert_severity: warn
```

Once a day, MMWatchdog on the node reads the end date. The first run within
180 days of the end date of regular security support sends a `warn` alert.
After an upgrade to a release with more than 180 days of regular security
support remaining, the first healthy run sends recovery.

## How it works

MMWatchdog reads `ID`, `ID_LIKE`, `VERSION_CODENAME`, and `PRETTY_NAME` from
`/etc/os-release`. Only `ID=debian` and `ID=ubuntu` select a dates file. A
node whose `ID` or `ID_LIKE` contains `suse` is a SUSE node, and a node whose
`ID` or `ID_LIKE` names `rhel`, `rocky`, `almalinux`, or `centos` is a node of
the Red Hat family.
`PRETTY_NAME` supplies the release name in the message.

MMWatchdog reads `/usr/share/distro-info/debian.csv` on Debian and
`/usr/share/distro-info/ubuntu.csv` on Ubuntu. The required input
`security_support` selects the deadline:

| `security_support` | Debian | Ubuntu |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `regular` | Debian's regular security support, `eol` | Ubuntu's standard security maintenance, `eol-server` |
| `debian_lts` | Debian LTS, `eol-lts` | Not allowed: the check is unknown |
| `ubuntu_pro` | Not allowed: the check is unknown | Ubuntu Pro's Expanded Security Maintenance, `eol-esm` |

A team that moves servers before Debian LTS takes over chooses `regular`.
A team content with Debian LTS's narrower package coverage chooses
`debian_lts`. A team whose Ubuntu nodes are attached to Ubuntu Pro chooses
`ubuntu_pro`. The check reads only the published dates: the check does not
verify that the node is attached to Ubuntu Pro, or that Debian LTS covers
the node's packages.

MMWatchdog finds columns by their header names, then finds the row whose
`series` equals `VERSION_CODENAME`. When the chosen end-date cell is empty,
MMWatchdog uses `eol`, such as for Ubuntu interim releases, which have no
`eol-server` or `eol-esm`. The message then says so, for example
`this node runs Ubuntu 25.10: the release has no end date of Ubuntu Pro's
Expanded Security Maintenance, and the release's support ends on 2026-07-09,
in 8 months`. A missing row or no usable end date makes the check unknown.

On a SUSE node, only `security_support: regular` applies. MMWatchdog reads
`/etc/products.d/baseproduct`, a link to the product file such as `Leap.prod`.
The end of the release is the `<endoflife>` element directly inside
`<product>`, such as `2028-11-30`. The `<endoflife>` inside `<codestream>` is
the end of the whole Leap 16 line, and the check does not use it. A missing
file, a missing `<endoflife>`, or an unreadable date makes the check
unknown. The message says `this node runs openSUSE Leap 16.1: SUSE's regular
security support ends on 2028-11-30, in 24 months`.

On a node of the Red Hat family, only `security_support: regular` applies. The
check reads `SUPPORT_END` from `/etc/os-release`, a date such as `2032-05-31`,
with or without quotes. The release package of the distribution installs the
file, and the vendor states in it the end of the release's updates: Rocky Linux
9.8 has `SUPPORT_END="2032-05-31"`, and AlmaLinux 10.2 has
`SUPPORT_END=2035-06-01`. Fedora 45 has `SUPPORT_END=2027-12-08`, the end of
that Fedora release, after which it gets no updates. A missing or unreadable
`SUPPORT_END` makes the check unknown. The message says `this node runs Rocky Linux 9.8 (Blue Onyx): the regular
security support that the release states ends on 2032-05-31, in 67 months`.

The date is `YYYY-MM-DD`, at 00:00 UTC. MMWatchdog subtracts the current
time from the end date of the chosen security support.
The check fails when the remaining time is no greater than
`fail_when_security_support_ends_within`.

## Errors and what they mean

| Message | What the message means, and what to do |
| --- | --- |
| `distribution_release_security_support.security_support: is required: ...` | State `regular`, `debian_lts`, or `ubuntu_pro` below the module name. |
| `security_support: debian_lts applies only to Debian, and this node runs NAME` | The value names the support of the other distribution. On Ubuntu, use `regular` or `ubuntu_pro`; on Debian, `regular` or `debian_lts`. |
| `distribution_release_security_support.fail_when_security_support_ends_within: is required: ...` | State a duration, such as `180d`, below the module name. |
| `MMWatchdog does not know the security support of NAME: it knows only that of Debian, Ubuntu, the Red Hat family, and SUSE` | The distribution's `ID` is neither `debian` nor `ubuntu`, neither `ID` nor `ID_LIKE` contains `suse`, and none names `rhel`, `rocky`, `almalinux`, or `centos`. A missing name is shown as `a distribution that /etc/os-release does not name`. |
| `/etc/os-release names no VERSION_CODENAME, so MMWatchdog cannot find the release of this node` | The node's release file has no codename. Check `/etc/os-release`. |
| `MMWatchdog cannot read PATH, which holds the dates of the releases: install the package distro-info-data` | The dates file is missing. Install `distro-info-data`. |
| `/etc/os-release gives no SUPPORT_END for this release, which the release package of NAME installs` | A node of the Red Hat family has no `SUPPORT_END` in `/etc/os-release`. Update the release package. |
| `MMWatchdog cannot read the SUPPORT_END of /etc/os-release: ERROR` | The `SUPPORT_END` is not a date `YYYY-MM-DD`. |
| `MMWatchdog cannot read PATH: ERROR` | The file cannot be read or parsed. Inspect the error and the installed package's file. |
| `MMWatchdog cannot read /etc/products.d/baseproduct, the product file of this release, which the release package of NAME installs` | A SUSE node has no product file. Check that the release package is installed. |
| `/etc/products.d/baseproduct gives no endoflife for this release` | The product file has no `<endoflife>` directly inside `<product>`. |
| `MMWatchdog cannot read the endoflife of /etc/products.d/baseproduct: ERROR` | The `<endoflife>` is not a date `YYYY-MM-DD`. |
| `PATH gives no end of SUPPORT for CODENAME: update the package distro-info-data` | The row or end date is missing. SUPPORT names the chosen support. Update `distro-info-data`; an unreleased release may have no date yet. |

## Tested on

[Limits on each distribution](../limits-on-each-distribution.md) says what MMWatchdog cannot do on each distribution, or did not test there, and why.

- **Go tests** in `server_checks_test.go`:
  `TestDistributionReleaseSecuritySupportCheck` covers healthy, approaching,
  and ended support; both support choices on Debian and Ubuntu; fallback
  dates and names; the threshold; and missing files, dates, rows, and
  codenames. `TestDistributionReleaseSecuritySupportCheckOnSUSE` in
  `suse_checks_test.go` covers the product file: healthy, within the
  threshold, ended, a file with both `<endoflife>` elements (the release's
  wins), without `<endoflife>`, with an unreadable date, and missing, and the
  other distributions' support values.
  `TestDistributionReleaseSecuritySupportCheckOnTheRedHatFamily` in
  `red_hat_checks_test.go` covers `SUPPORT_END` healthy, within the threshold
  (with quotes, as Rocky Linux writes it), ended, missing, unreadable, and the
  other distributions' support values. `TestDistributionReleaseSecuritySupportCheckOnFedora`
  in `fedora_checks_test.go` covers Fedora's `ID` and its `SUPPORT_END`.
  `TestUpdateChecksOnUnknownDistributions` covers unsupported
  distributions, including Linux Mint. Input validation accepts both support
  choices and rejects missing support, a wrong support value, a missing
  duration, or `soon`.
- **The node suite** (`node_scenarios.py`) tests
  `distribution_release_security_support` on the Debian, Ubuntu, and
  openSUSE Leap releases, and on Rocky Linux 9, AlmaLinux 10, and Fedora 45, of [every target distribution](../../changing-mmwatchdog/testing.md#every-target-distribution).
  On Arch Linux, the suite checks only that the check is
  unknown and that its message names the distribution. On openSUSE Leap, the
  suite reads `<endoflife>` from the product file with Python's XML parser and
  compares it with the check's date, status, and message.
  On Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, and Fedora, the suite reads `SUPPORT_END` with the shell and
  compares it with the check's date, status, and message, and removes the line
  to check the unknown result.
  The node suite installs `distro-info-data` when missing, then moves the
  dates file away on the test guest and checks for an unknown result.
  The suite reads the support end date independently from the test guest's
  dates file, by the column's name.

  For both support choices with `180d`, the check must match the status
  calculated from the date. Ended support fails at any lead time. With
  `3650d`, a support choice whose date is more than 180 days away must fail.
  Each message must name the selected support or fallback, the end date
  read by the suite, and the test guest's `PRETTY_NAME`.
- The latest run passed on every target distribution
  ([validation record](../../changing-mmwatchdog/validation.md)).

## Why it works this way

- **The check names the support explicitly.** A reader of the check sees
  which security support deadline the check counts down to.
- **Debian LTS differs from regular security support.** A separate team
  runs Debian LTS, with fewer packages covered. A team may need to move
  servers before regular security support ends.
- **The chosen support can end while apt still reports no waiting updates.**
  [`apt_security_updates`](apt_security_updates.md) reports updates
  that wait to be installed, but cannot warn that security support has ended.
- **Each value names one support.** On Ubuntu, a value such as
  `long_term` would read like an Ubuntu LTS release, whose support is what
  `regular` counts down to. `debian_lts` and `ubuntu_pro` name the support
  itself, and a value of the other distribution makes the check unknown
  rather than guessing.
- **The check does not count down to Debian's paid Extended LTS
  (`eol-elts`) or Ubuntu's paid Legacy Support (`eol-legacy`).** Both extend
  support beyond `debian_lts` and `ubuntu_pro`. A value for them can be added
  when a team needs one.
- **Installed release data needs no network request.** The release dates
  stay current when apt installs updates to `distro-info-data` alongside
  updates to the node's other packages. A missing date is unknown, never
  proof of continuing support.
- **Derivatives have their own support policies.** `ID_LIKE` cannot prove
  that a derivative gets fixes until Debian's or Ubuntu's end date.
- **SUSE's end date is the release's, not the line's.** The product file of
  Leap 16.1 holds the end of Leap 16.1 itself and, in `<codestream>`, the end
  of the whole Leap 16 line, which is later. A node that moves to the next
  Leap 16 release must move before the release's own end date.
- **SUSE has one value, `regular`.** The product file gives one end date.
  `debian_lts` and `ubuntu_pro` are the support of other distributions, so
  they make the check unknown rather than guess.
